title: Om gam ganapataye
hook: Ganesha's mantra; why even Shiva begins with him
carry: begin with ganesha: gam, his seed sound

segments.voice: Yesterday, Appar's floating stone and the panchakshara, Om Namah Shivaya. Your line was om namah shivaya: Shiva's name is a refuge. Today, Shiva's son, and the mantra for starting things.
screen: `OM NAMAH SHIVAYA: SHIVA'S NAME IS A REFUGE.`

segments.voice: A new shop opens in Delhi, and before the first customer walks in, there's a small picture of Ganesha by the till with a garland on it. A student in Chennai writes Shri Ganesh at the top of an exam paper before the first answer. A new car gets a little Ganesha on the dashboard. Whatever is starting, he's there first. You've heard how Shiva promised his son would be worshipped first. Here's the day the promise was tested, on Shiva himself.
screen: `A NEW SHOP, A NEW EXAM.` → `A NEW CAR.` → `GANESHA IS THERE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Ganesha's own Purana tells it, and a temple in Tamil Nadu is named for it. Shiva sets out to destroy Tripura, three flying cities of demons that only a single arrow could ever bring down. The whole universe becomes his war chariot: the earth for its body, the sun and moon for its wheels. And Shiva, in a hurry, doesn't stop to honor Ganesha. The axle snaps. The great god stands there with his bow, going nowhere. So Shiva does what everyone else does. He honors his son first. The chariot rolls, and the three cities fall to one arrow. Even the god who made the promise keeps it. That's why so many Hindu rituals open with Ganesha, even a puja to another god. One of his names is Vighneshvara, lord of obstacles: he removes them, and some say he also places them, when a road shouldn't be taken yet. And the way many people ask is this mantra: Om Gam Ganapataye Namah. Om, the sound of everything. Gam, a bija, a seed syllable. In Hindu mantra practice, a bija isn't a word about a god; many hold that it carries the god inside it, the way a seed holds a tree. Gam is Ganesha's seed. Ganapataye: to Ganapati, lord of the hosts. Namah: I bow. So the Ganesha on the dashboard, the Shri Ganesh at the top of a page, the gam said quietly before a first day or a hard conversation: it's the lesson of the broken axle. Begin with Ganesha.
screen: `EVEN SHIVA FORGOT ONCE.` · `THE AXLE SNAPS.` · `VIGHNESHVARA, LORD OF OBSTACLES.` · `GAM — GANESHA'S SEED SYLLABLE.` · then, large: `BEGIN WITH GANESHA: GAM.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind one thing you're about to begin, this week, tomorrow, even the next hour. Then, on beads or finger joints, do japa twenty-seven times: Om Gam Ganapataye Namah, slowly, letting the gam land softly, like something set down at a doorway. If you don't pray, let it be sound and counting, with the thing you're beginning in view, and at twenty-seven, rest.
Bija, a seed syllable that holds a deity inside it: gam, Ganesha's seed, in the mantra Om Gam Ganapataye, said before beginnings.
Take this with you: begin with Ganesha, gam, his seed sound. Even Shiva starts there. Day one hundred six, done.

howItsDone: Hindus commonly invoke Ganesha before beginning anything: a puja, a journey, a business, a wedding, an exam. Om Gam Ganapataye Namah is chanted in japa, often 108 times, in many regions especially on Wednesdays and on Ganesh Chaturthi.
